query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the Co‐free FeNiCrMn high‐entropy alloy, dynamic deformation (across a range of temperatures and strain rates) induces a controlled, strain‐rate–dependent amorphization at the grain boundaries that creates an ultra‐nanocrystalline near‐surface layer. This dynamic structural reorganization mediates dislocation motion in a way that enhances ductility without sacrificing strength, thereby explaining the observed favorable strength–ductility balance relative to the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, solid-solution Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi with a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Applying controlled deformation at different strain rates and temperatures during mechanical testing.
generation.conditions: Tests performed under inert or ultra-high vacuum conditions to minimize oxidation effects, with strain rates and temperatures within the regime where dynamic amorphization is predicted to occur.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer mediated by strain-activated dynamic amorphization at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under dynamic loading, the grain boundaries reorganize through an amorphization process that refines the effective grain size (i.e., inverse Hall-Petch behavior). This transformation reduces barriers to dislocation motion while also providing enhanced work hardening, leading to the optimal strength–ductility balance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline of lower strain rate or room-temperature conditions, tests at higher strain rates and elevated temperatures will show a measurable reduction in effective grain size (verified via STEM), lower friction coefficients, and a maintained or improved strength–ductility balance. Specifically, alloys exhibiting the dynamic formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline layer will display lower wear rates and altered mechanical properties consistent with inverse Hall-Petch trends.
generation.baseline: The mechanical and microstructural behavior of the alloy under relatively low strain rate and ambient temperature conditions, where the dynamic amorphous transformation is less pronounced.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies within a temperature and strain rate regime where dynamic amorphization is active (e.g., temperatures high enough to promote boundary mobility but below levels that trigger full recrystallization, and strain rates sufficiently high to induce dynamic layer formation without thermal overrun). It may not hold in highly oxidizing environments or at extreme temperatures where other mechanisms (e.g., diffusion-dominated processes) predominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between strain rate, temperature, and the degree of dynamic amorphization (and subsequent nano-layer formation) is uncertain. Additionally, the interplay between ductility and strength under these conditions may involve secondary factors not fully captured in this hypothesis.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one of the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy and one of the baseline equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy. Subject both sets to a series of mechanical tests at varying strain rates and temperatures within the defined regime (under inert or ultra-high vacuum conditions). Post-deformation, characterize the near-surface microstructure using high-resolution STEM to assess the presence and thickness of an ultra-nanocrystalline layer, and measure mechanical properties (strength, ductility, friction coefficients, and wear rates).
measurements: Grain size and phase identification via STEM before and after deformation
Stress–strain curves to determine strength and ductility
Friction coefficient and wear rate measurements during/after deformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy does not exhibit a significant formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline layer (relative to the baseline) under high strain rate and elevated temperature conditions, and/or if no corresponding improvement or balance in strength–ductility along with lower friction and wear rates is observed compared with the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
